title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Introduction
content: The mammillary bodies are paired brainstem nuclei situated on the posteroinferior aspect of the hypothalamus. One mammillary body lies on each side of the midline. Early anatomists named these structures after mammary tissue because of their rounded appearance resembling small breasts (see Image . Mammillary Bodies). [1]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Introduction
content: The mammillary bodies play a critical role in memory consolidation, with lesions producing profound cognitive deficits. Surgical interventions in the hypothalamic and limbic regions require a precise understanding of the position of these paired structures to avoid iatrogenic injury. Familiarity with the connections and functional circuitry of the mammillary bodies assists clinicians in correlating anatomical findings with clinical presentation and imaging.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The mammillary bodies constitute one of the primary nuclei within the Papez circuit. This circuit facilitates consolidation and storage of spatial, episodic, and working memory. [2] [3] Different types of memory are transmitted through distinct subregions and circuits. [4] Lesions of the fornix or mammillary bodies disrupt these circuits and produce amnesia. [5] [6] The mammillary bodies also contribute to emotion, reward, and goal-directed behaviors. [7]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The principal function of the mammillary bodies is recollective memory. Memory information originates in the hippocampus, where θ waves activate CA3 neurons. Information is conveyed through the fornix to the mammillary bodies. Projections from the mammillary bodies reach the anterior thalamic nuclei via the mammillothalamic tract. The anterior thalamic nuclei project to the cingulate cortex, which, in turn, projects to the entorhinal cortex. A bidirectional projection between the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex completes the Papez circuit.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The mammillary bodies also participate in spatial memory. Projections from the dorsal subiculum reach the medial mammillary bodies bilaterally, with collateral projections to the retrosplenial cortex and entorhinal cortex. Medial mammillary body projections are activated during movement, stimulating locomotion and initiating place aversion. [8] These circuits are essential for accurate navigation in rodent models. [9] Although the specific roles of individual pathways remain incompletely defined, the organization of the circuit contributes substantially to spatial memory, cognition, and emotion. [10]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: Beyond transmitting memory information, the mammillary bodies facilitate the formation of appropriate behavioral responses through reciprocal connections with the tegmentum. The medial mammillary nucleus projects bidirectionally to the ventral tegmental area. The lateral mammillary nucleus projects bidirectionally to the dorsal tegmental nucleus. The ventral tegmentum contains a high density of dopamine neurons and functions as a reward center of the brain.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: Memory information from the hippocampus integrates with signals regarding the reward or aversive properties of specific stimuli or stimulus sets in the environment, enabling the processing of stimulus salience. [11] The mammillary bodies transmit information about reward or aversion via the anterior thalamic nucleus to the cingulate cortex, where this information contributes to the formation of emotional perception.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The dorsal tegmental connections to the lateral mammillary nucleus function to process goal-directed movement. The dorsal tegmental nucleus is located between the trochlear nuclei within the midbrain. [12] Neurons in the dorsal tegmental nucleus respond specifically to movement velocity, turning behaviors, and learned goal-directed behaviors. Direct connections exist between the dorsal tegmental nucleus and the ventral tegmental nucleus, guiding processing in the reward circuit and facilitating improved goal-directed behaviors. [13]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The mammillary bodies transmit this stream of information to the cerebellum. This connection is hypothesized to support the cerebellum's role in visuospatial orientation, movement learning, and motor memory. Disruption of information flow between the cerebellum and mammillary bodies may contribute to navigational impairments during the early stages of neurodegenerative disorders. [14]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: The mammillary bodies lack interneurons. Information processing within the mammillary bodies occurs via interconnections from projection neurons originating in other brain regions. Reciprocal dopaminergic and cholinergic projections from the tegmentum help regulate the information transmitted from the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nucleus (Papez circuit) and the cerebellum.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Structure and Function
content: Reciprocal tegmental connections enable mammillary activity to influence the tegmentum and its associated structures, including the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and nucleus accumbens. Activation of the acetylcholine and dopamine circuits triggers downstream engagement of norepinephrine and serotonin systems. These neurotransmitter systems contribute to cortical memory storage and support other limbic functions, such as attention, learning, memory, motor coordination, decision-making, planning, and emotion.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Embryology
content: The mammillary bodies arise from the ectoderm during development. The ectoderm forms the neural tube, which closes at 6 weeks of gestation. The neural tube differentiates into the forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord. The forebrain develops into the telencephalon and diencephalon. The hypothalamus, mammillary bodies, and posterior pituitary originate from the diencephalon. [15]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Mammillary bodies receive blood supply from the circle of Willis, located on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus. Branches of the posteromedial artery directly supply the mammillary bodies. These arteries arise from the posterior cerebral artery or, alternatively, from the posterior communicating artery. The posteromedial artery consists of 3 branches: rostral, deep penetrating, and caudal. The caudal branches specifically supply the mammillary bodies.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The capillary plexus in this region drains blood from the mammillary bodies through the hypothalamo-neurohypophysial portal system. Blood flows from the portal system into the cavernous sinus and continues through either the superior or inferior petrosal sinuses to enter the jugular vein.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Lymphatics within the brain differ from those in other regions of the body. The blood-brain barrier regulates the movement and transport of nutrients, small molecules, metabolites, cells, and toxins into and out of the brain.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The blood-brain barrier is a functional and structural boundary between the vasculature and the brain, formed by brain endothelial cells, adjacent astrocytic end-feet, and pericytes. Tight junctions connect endothelial cells, creating a physical barrier that forces most molecules to travel through selective transcellular routes, forming a transport barrier. A synergistic relationship exists between brain endothelial cells and astrocytes. Perivascular astrocytic end-feet surround endothelial cells, separated by a basal lamina. This combined barrier protects the brain from toxins and facilitates the transport of nutrients, waste products, glucose, lipids, and neurotransmitters between capillaries and neurons. [16]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Nerves
content: Mammillary bodies have 3 major direct connections: hippocampus, thalamus, and tegmental nuclei. The hippocampus projects to the mammillary bodies via afferent fibers in the fornix. The mammillary bodies process memory-related information and relay it to the thalamus through the mammillothalamic tract, which terminates within the anterior thalamic nuclei. Both hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies and projections from the mammillary bodies to the thalamus are unidirectional. These circuits form part of the Papez circuit. Mammillary bodies also establish bidirectional connections with the tegmental nuclei through the mammillotegmental tract. Extensive tegmental connections with multiple limbic structures allow mammillary body input to influence a variety of limbic functions (see above).

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Muscles
content: Although the mammillary bodies do not directly contact muscle, they project to the cerebellum, a secondary motor brain region. Inputs from the tegmentum carry information about movement velocity, turning behaviors, and learned goal-directed behaviors. The mammillary bodies also receive memory information from the hippocampus and stimulus salience signals from the tegmentum. These inputs suggest a role for the mammillary bodies in supporting cerebellar motor learning functions.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Physiologic Variants
content: The mammillary bodies are part of the hypothalamus. The physiology of this region is critical for survival. Consequently, only a few developmental or physiological variations are compatible with fetal viability.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Physiologic Variants
content: Throughout life, the mammillary bodies adapt to environmental and physiological changes, enabling alterations in behavior based on the learned salience of a stimulus or stimulus set. Although adaptation to environmental stimuli is beneficial, neurons and connections of the mammillary bodies remain vulnerable to damage from environmental factors, such as alcohol exposure or thiamine deficiency. [17] These factors, together with aging-related neurodegeneration, can markedly affect mammillary circuit function. [18]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Surgical Considerations
content: Surgeons use the mammillary bodies as landmarks during procedures involving the hypothalamus or the 3rd ventricle. In patients with noncommunicating hydrocephalus, ventriculostomy is performed to relieve pressure. During these procedures, the space between the mammillary bodies and the dorsum sellae provides access to the 3rd ventricle. [19] [20]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Surgical Considerations
content: The mammillary bodies can shift in patients with craniopharyngiomas involving the hypothalamus. The angle between the base of the mammillary bodies and the floor of the 4th ventricle on midsagittal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicates tumor location. Angles less than 60° correspond to a tuberal-interventricular tumor, whereas angles greater than 90° indicate tumor invagination of the 3rd ventricle. Therefore, mammillary body position serves as a rapid reference for tumor localization, providing surgeons with information to guide management. [21]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Clinical Significance
content: Damage to the mammillary bodies can result from trauma, stroke, tumors, or environmental factors, such as thiamine deficiency or chronic alcoholism. [22] Thiamine deficiency is a common cause of Korsakoff syndrome. This condition may occur in conjunction with Wernicke encephalopathy, which is often induced by chronic alcoholism through thiamine depletion, dietary deficiencies, or impaired gut absorption. [23] In both disorders, these factors produce bilateral degeneration of mammillary body neurons or projections. Bilateral damage leads to anterograde amnesia, which can occur independently or alongside additional symptoms, including reckless behavior, reduced motivation, and confabulation. [24]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Clinical Significance
content: Wernicke encephalopathy represents an acute neurological emergency that may be reversed with thiamine treatment. The condition presents with a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and altered mental status. Untreated Wernicke encephalopathy may progress to chronic Korsakoff syndrome, at which point amnesia symptoms are often irreversible. [25] T2-weighted MRI with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and diffusion-weighted imaging detects acute encephalopathy, whereas chronic mammillary body atrophy is better visualized with volumetric T1-weighted imaging. [26]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Other Issues
content: The mammillary bodies and their associated circuits, including limbic structures, influence numerous higher-order functions. Stimulation of the Papez circuit has been hypothesized to improve memory and attention while reducing the incidence of depression in individuals with dementia. In animal models, deep-brain stimulation of the hippocampus enhances memory function without inducing anxiety. These effects are attributed to increased activation of the cingulate gyrus via the hippocampus-mammillary tract, the mammillothalamic tract, and thalamic projections to the cingulate gyrus, the brain region responsible for emotion perception. [27]

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Other Issues
content: Deep brain stimulation has been used to treat Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and dementia. [28] [29] [30] Optimal results occur when the stimulation probe is positioned near the fornix to activate hippocampal fibers projecting to the mammillary bodies. [31] These treatments have modified the rate of brain atrophy in individuals with Alzheimer disease. [32] The mechanisms by which Papez circuit activation slows atrophy are unknown. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that deep brain stimulation of the Papez circuit may represent a viable clinical approach for individuals with various psychiatric or dementia-related disorders.

title: Neuroanatomy, Mammillary Bodies -- Other Issues
content: Using 7T MRI, researchers have observed hypothalamic enlargement in patients with mood disorders. Although the mammillary bodies were hypothesized to contribute to this dysfunction, no enlargement of the mammillary bodies was detected. Consequently, the precise contribution of mammillary body circuits to mood disorders remains unclear.
